context: protection & energisation-led · staged testing proves the power apparatus

brief.intro: An electrical substation or switchyard transforms power between voltage levels and switches it safely along the grid. Its build is dominated by heavy power apparatus — transformers, switchgear — an extensive earthing/grounding grid, and a protection & control system that must be proven point-by-point before anything is energised. Unlike a typical building, structural and civil works exist mainly to support and enable the equipment: foundations, cable trenches and oil-containment bunds. The real programme risk sits in equipment delivery, earthing-grid verification, and a staged energisation sequence that only the grid/network operator can authorise. Air-insulated switchgear (AIS, open-air) and gas-insulated switchgear (GIS, compact and SF6-insulated) follow different erection logic, but both converge on the same commissioning backbone: protection relay testing, SCADA point-to-point, and staged energisation up to full load.

scope.name: Earthworks & site preparation
scope.desc: Grading, drainage, access roads and the yard surface (often stone/gravel) for step-touch potential control.

scope.name: Earthing / grounding grid
scope.desc: The buried copper grid bonding every structure and item of equipment to a common reference, tested for step-and-touch potential.

scope.name: Foundations & structural steel
scope.desc: Equipment plinths, gantries and structure steel for busbars and overhead-line entries.

scope.name: Power transformers
scope.desc: Main power transformers, their foundations, oil-containment bunds and cooling systems.

scope.name: HV/MV switchgear (AIS or GIS)
scope.desc: Circuit breakers, disconnectors and busbars — air-insulated outdoor or gas-insulated indoor.

scope.name: Protection, control & SCADA
scope.desc: Relay panels, control-building wiring and remote telemetry to the network control centre.

scope.name: Cabling & containment
scope.desc: Power and control cable trenches/ducts linking equipment to the control building.

scope.name: Control building
scope.desc: Houses protection/control panels, battery/DC systems and operator facilities.

scope.name: Fire protection & auxiliary systems
scope.desc: Transformer fire suppression/deluge, control-building HVAC, lighting.

scope.name: Testing, staged energisation & commissioning
scope.desc: Protection point-to-point, HV testing, earthing verification, staged energisation to the network.

glossary.plain: Air-Insulated Switchgear — open-air, bigger footprint — versus Gas-Insulated Switchgear — compact, SF6-insulated, usually indoors.
a buried copper mesh bonding everything to earth so a fault doesn't create a dangerous step-and-touch voltage.
the device that detects a fault and trips the right breaker fast enough to protect equipment and the grid.
verifying every single control/protection wire goes from the right source to the right destination before anything is live.
a transformer protection device that senses gas buildup or oil surges from an internal fault.
bringing the substation live in planned steps — no-load, then load — under utility/grid-operator authorisation, not all at once.
the voltage a person could experience standing near or touching equipment during a fault; the earthing grid is designed and tested to keep it safe.

must_get_right: Prove the earthing grid — continuity plus step-and-touch potential test — before any equipment energisation; it's a safety prerequisite, not a formality.
Sequence protection-relay and SCADA point-to-point testing to finish before staged energisation — energising with unproven protection is a safety and asset risk.
Coordinate staged-energisation dates with the grid/network operator early — the final energisation steps are often on their schedule, not the contractor's, and can't be compressed.
Order transformers and GIS/AIS switchgear immediately — they are the longest-lead items and set the whole programme's finish date.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities carry durations in working days; the network is calculated (F9) with no artificial constraints beyond contractual milestones. Total float is kept ≥ 0 in the baseline.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Civil and structural steel run a 6-day week; earthing-grid installation and cable pulling move to two shifts at peak to protect the critical path; HV testing and staged energisation follow the network/grid operator's outage and switching windows, which may fall outside normal working calendars.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs transformer/switchgear procurement → foundations & earthing grid → equipment erection → cable termination → protection & SCADA point-to-point → HV testing → staged energisation (no-load, then on-load) authorised by the network operator. The earthing grid must be installed and step-touch tested before any equipment is energised, and protection relay setting/testing must be complete before HV testing begins.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Single-line diagram and protection philosophy are frozen before switchgear/relay ordering; a single mobilisation; the grid/network operator's outage windows for tie-ins and staged energisation are secured in advance; and no late change to voltage class or fault-level rating that would resize transformers or switchgear.

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Transformer delivery requires heavy-haul transport routes and crane/jacking capacity to set on foundation; earthing works need dry-season trenching to avoid groundwater interference with resistivity testing. Staged energisation is constrained by the network operator's switching/outage schedule, which is often the true limiting resource late in the programme, not site labour.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: transformer/GIS delivery slippage, earthing-grid step-touch test failures requiring rework, and staged-energisation dates slipping against the network operator's outage windows. Schedule contingency is held immediately before HV testing and before staged energisation rather than spread across erection activities.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the field — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
